transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Well, it's... it's a bit hard to talk about, but I guess I'm here because of what's been happening in the evenings. You see, I sell insurance, which is a lot of sitting at a desk and talking on the phone, and I really, really try to be so good during the day. I'm very strict with myself from the moment I wake up—I'll just have something small, keep it very disciplined. But then... then I get home after work, and it's like a switch just flips in my brain. 

I'll walk in the door, put my purse down, and I just start eating, and I end up eating way, way more than I ever intended to. It usually starts out okay, just making a normal dinner, but then... then I'll have a bowl of cereal. And then I'll open a box of crackers. And then I'm digging into whatever leftovers are sitting in the fridge, and then I absolutely have to have something sweet, so I'm finding cookies or whatever sweets I have around the kitchen... and this all happens so fast, just all within a couple of hours. I just keep going, and it's really starting to bother me because, like I said, I try so hard to be strict all day, and then the evening just completely falls apart on me.
How do you feel after these episodes of eating in the evenings?

Well, it's... it's just this awful, defeated feeling, honestly. Because while it's happening, once I get started on those nights, it's like... it's like I'm not even the one driving anymore. I'll be standing there, maybe leaning against the counter where I put my keys and the mail down, and I'll actually be telling myself in my head, "Okay, that's enough, you don't need any more, just go sit in the living room and turn on the TV." But it's like I can't even listen to my own voice. 

I just keep going back to the kitchen, opening the pantry, checking the fridge again, even while I'm practically begging myself to just stop and walk away. It's so frustrating because I know better, you know? But I don't really feel back in charge of myself until... well, until it's over, and by then I'm just so uncomfortably full. 

My stomach will actually be aching because I've just stuffed so much in there so fast, mixing all those different foods together. And then, after that switch finally flips back and I'm in control again, I just have to sit there with that heavy, stretched-out feeling in my stomach. I end up looking at the empty cracker boxes or the dishes on the counter, and I just get so mad at myself. I think about how disciplined I was all day at the office, and then I just feel so ashamed that I couldn't stop myself until I was physically too full to keep going. It just ruins the whole rest of my night.
Do you feel like you're eating much more quickly than usual during these episodes?

Well, I'm not really sure if it's faster, exactly. I mean, I guess I've never really timed myself or thought about the speed of it all. It's more about the sheer volume and the feeling of not being able to stop, you know? Like, when I come home and put my purse down on that little table by the door—the one with the mail and the keys—I just kind of drift into the kitchen. And once I start, it's just a continuous motion. 

I wouldn't say I'm, like, shoveling it in at a breakneck pace or anything. It's just that I keep going. I'll have the cereal, and then I'll find the crackers, and then I'm looking for the cookies. It's just one thing after another. So, I don't know if the actual chewing and swallowing part is faster than when I eat my little disciplined lunch at my desk at the insurance office... it's just that there aren't any breaks. I don't sit down and savor it or chat with anyone. It's just this steady, relentless grazing until I'm so full my stomach aches. So, yeah, I haven't really noticed if I'm eating quicker, just that I'm eating a lot more and I can't seem to make myself stop until I'm completely stuffed.
Do you feel guilty after these episodes of eating in the evenings are over?

Well, you know, I'm not really sure if "guilty" is the right word for it. I mean, I know I just said a few minutes ago that I feel ashamed and I get mad at myself, which I absolutely do, but... guilt? Guilt feels like something else entirely to me. 

Like, at my job, if I were to accidentally give a client the wrong quote on their auto insurance, or if I forgot to file a claim for them and it caused them a bunch of financial trouble, then I would definitely feel guilty, because I hurt somebody else, you know? I let them down and it affected their life. 

But with this... with the eating in the evenings... it's really just me. I'm just standing there in my own kitchen, usually by myself, looking at the empty cracker boxes and the dirty bowls left on the counter. I haven't hurt anyone else. So I don't really feel like I've committed a crime or done something wrong to another person that I need to feel guilty about. It's more just this... this intense, overwhelming frustration with my own lack of willpower. I'll be standing there, looking at the mess, thinking about how I was so incredibly good all day at the office, eating my little disciplined lunch while I made my calls, and then I just threw all that hard work away the second I walked through my own front door. 

So, no, I haven't really noticed feeling guilty, exactly. It's just... I'm just so annoyed that I have to go to the grocery store again to replace the things I ate, and I'm just tired of having that heavy, stretched-out feeling in my stomach. But guilt... no, I don't think I'd call it that. I'm just really, really mad at myself for not being able to just sit on the couch and watch TV like a normal person.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you start during these evenings?

Well, yes, absolutely. I think I mentioned this a little bit earlier, but it's like... once I cross that threshold, once I've put my keys down on that little table and I drift into the kitchen, it's just this overwhelming feeling that I'm not the one steering the ship anymore. 

It's the strangest thing, because I'll literally be standing there, looking at the open pantry, and my own internal voice—the same voice that was so perfectly disciplined all day at the insurance office, the one that tells me exactly what to say to clients—that voice is practically screaming at me, "Okay, that's enough, you don't need any more, just go sit in the living room." But it's like I can't even hear it, or I hear it but my hands just won't listen. I just keep going back. I'll close the fridge, walk away for a second, and then I'm right back opening it again. 

I'm practically begging myself to just stop and walk away, but I can't. It's a complete loss of control. I don't feel like I'm back in charge of my own body, my own actions, until the whole thing is over. And by the time that switch finally flips and I'm me again, I'm just so uncomfortably full. It's like I have to reach that point of physical discomfort, where my stomach is actually aching from being so stretched out, before I can finally put the brakes on. It's just so frustrating to know what I should be doing and just be completely unable to make myself do it.
Do you usually feel stressed, anxious, or upset before these episodes of eating in the evenings start?

Well, I've thought about that, you know, because you read articles in magazines or see things on TV about "stress eating" or "emotional eating," and it always seems like there's some big, dramatic trigger. Like someone gets fired or goes through a terrible breakup, and then they're sitting on the floor with a tub of ice cream crying their eyes out. But for me... it's really not like that at all. 

I don't think I feel particularly stressed or anxious right before it happens. I mean, my job at the insurance office has its moments—sometimes a client gets upset about a premium increase, or the computers go down right when I'm trying to pull up a quote—but honestly, by the time I leave work, I'm usually just... done. I'm not carrying a bunch of anxiety home with me. The drive home is usually pretty quiet, I listen to the radio, maybe think about what errands I need to run over the weekend. 

It's not like I walk through the door feeling upset or on edge. It's more just... a routine, I guess? It's like my brain just shifts gears the second I put my keys on that little table. I don't feel sad, I don't feel angry, I don't feel overwhelmed by my day. It's almost like I don't feel much of anything right before it starts. It's just this magnetic pull to the kitchen. So, no, I wouldn't say there's a big wave of emotion or stress that sets it off. It just sort of... happens, regardless of whether I had a perfectly fine Tuesday or a mildly annoying Wednesday. It's just what I do when I get home.
Does this loss of control over eating ever happen to you at other times of the day, or is it mostly in the evenings?

No, no, it's really just the evenings. During the day, I'm completely fine. Honestly, it's like night and day—no pun intended! Because at the office, I have my routine, you know? I pack my little lunch in the morning—usually just a sensible salad with some grilled chicken, or maybe a turkey wrap—and I eat it right at my desk while I'm reviewing auto policies or returning client calls. There's no urge, no loss of control at all. I feel completely, one hundred percent in charge. I'll even turn down donuts if someone brings them into the breakroom for a birthday, and I won't even think twice about it. I just sip my water and go about my business.

But then... well, it's exactly like I was trying to explain a minute ago about when I get home. It's so specific to the evening. Once I get started on those nights, it's like I just keep going back to the kitchen, over and over again, even while I'm actively telling myself to stop. I'll still have my work shoes on, just pacing between the living room and the pantry, and my brain is saying, "You don't need this, you're not even hungry, just go sit down," but I just keep reaching for things. 

It's like I'm on autopilot and someone else programmed the destination. I really don't feel like I'm back in charge of myself until I hit that point where I'm just uncomfortably full. It’s like my stomach has to physically ache and stretch before the spell finally breaks and I'm me again, and I can finally just stop and walk away from the counter. But before 6 PM? Never happens. It's strictly an evening thing.
Do you feel like you've done something wrong after these eating episodes are over?

Oh, gosh, yes. Absolutely. The guilt is just... it's immense. It's like this heavy, wet blanket just drops right over me the very second that spell breaks and I realize what I've just done. I'll be standing there in the kitchen, or maybe I've finally made it to the couch, and I just look at the empty boxes or the wrappers, and I just think, "Why? Why did you do this again?" It's this awful, sinking feeling of failure, really, because I know better. I'm a fifty-year-old woman, I manage complex insurance policies all day, I should be able to manage my own dinner, right? So, yes, I feel like I've done something terribly wrong. 

And because I feel so guilty, so ashamed of it, I always... well, I have this whole routine the next day to try and fix it. I'll tell myself I'm making up for it. So the next morning, I'll wake up and I'll just completely skip breakfast. Won't even look at the toaster. And then at the office—you know how I mentioned my sensible little salads or turkey wraps earlier? Well, after one of those bad nights, I won't even pack that. I'll just skip lunch entirely. I'll sit at my desk, and maybe my stomach is actually growling by 1 or 2 PM while I'm on the phone with a client, but I'll just drink ice water and ignore it, telling myself I don't need food after what I did the night before. 

And it doesn't even stop with the food, either. I feel like I have to physically work it off. So I'll force myself to take an extra-long hike. There's this trail system near my neighborhood, and usually I'd just do the short loop, but I'll make myself do the steep, two-hour trail, even if it's hot out and my legs feel like lead. Or... oh, I play in this women's slow-pitch softball league. It's usually a lot of fun, most of the ladies are around my age, but we do have these conditioning practices. If I had a bad episode the night before, I will push myself so much harder at softball conditioning. I'll run extra bases, I'll push through the drills, even when I am just completely, bone-deep tired and my body is begging me to stop. I just get it in my head that I have to burn it all off, that I have to pay the penance for losing control. It's just this exhausting cycle of messing up and then punishing myself the whole next day to try and wipe the slate clean.
Do you often restrict your food intake to very low calories or skip meals altogether on days following these episodes?

Yes, exactly, that's... well, that's exactly what I was just getting at. It's almost like a strict rule I have for myself now. The very next day after one of those nights, I'll wake up and immediately tell myself that I'm making up for it. I won't even look at food. Skipping breakfast and lunch isn't just something that happens because I'm busy with clients or distracted at the office—it's very, very intentional. 

Like I was saying about sitting at my desk with just my ice water? I'll sit there, pulling up auto quotes or dealing with underwriting, and my stomach will be absolutely twisting in knots because it's empty, but I just refuse to eat. I tell myself, "You had more than enough last night, you don't get to eat today." 

And then, on top of practically eating zero calories all day, I'll still force myself out onto that steep hiking trail, or I'll go to the softball field and just run myself ragged. I'll push so much harder at conditioning, doing those extra sprints between the bases even when my legs are shaking and I'm just completely, utterly tired. I just feel this intense need to balance the scales, you know? To erase the night before. So, yes, restricting what I eat to practically nothing and exercising until I drop is exactly what happens the whole next day. It's exhausting, honestly, but I just can't seem to let myself off the hook.
Do you ever make yourself vomit after one of these episodes of eating in the evenings?

No, no, I don't do that. I know some people do, but that's just... I've never been able to bring myself to do that. The thought of it just makes me feel awful. I mean, my stomach will be hurting so much, just stretched tight like a drum, and I'll be sitting there on the couch, feeling so incredibly full and miserable, and maybe a part of me wishes I could just undo it right then and there. But making myself throw up? No. I just can't. 

I actually hate throwing up. Even when I get the stomach flu—which, thankfully, isn't very often, maybe once every few years, usually if someone brings a bug into the office and we're all sharing the same coffee pot—I fight it as long as I can. I'll just lie there with a cool washcloth on my forehead, sipping ginger ale, doing everything in my power not to be sick. So the idea of doing it on purpose, night after night? No, that's not me at all. 

That's why I rely so heavily on the skipping meals and the exercise the next day. Because since I can't—or won't—make myself sick to get rid of the food right away, I feel like I have to work twice as hard the next day to burn it off. That's why I'll push myself on that two-hour hike, or run those extra bases at softball practice until my lungs are burning. It's my way of purging it, I guess, just not... not the physical throwing up way. I just sweat it out and starve it out instead. But vomiting? No, never.
Do you ever use laxatives or diuretics to try and undo the effects of one of these eating episodes?

No, no, I've never touched those either. I mean, I know what they are, of course. You see the commercials for them, or you walk down the pharmacy aisle at Walgreens when you're just trying to pick up some allergy medicine or maybe some cotton balls, and there they are. But I've never bought them. I've never even been tempted to, honestly. 

It's sort of like the throwing up thing, I guess. Taking a pill to force my body to... well, to get rid of it that way... it just feels so unnatural and, honestly, a bit scary. I have this coworker, Brenda, she sits a few cubicles down from me, and she used to take these water pills—diuretics, I guess—because she said they helped her feel less bloated before big events. She took them before her daughter's wedding last spring. But she ended up feeling so dizzy and lightheaded at work one afternoon that we almost had to call someone. She was just sitting at her desk, white as a sheet, and I remember thinking, "I am never putting myself in that position." I need to be sharp for my clients. I can't be passing out in the middle of explaining a comprehensive auto policy because I took some pill to make me lose water weight. 

And laxatives? Oh, gosh, no. The idea of having my stomach cramping up like that, or being tied to the bathroom all day... I just couldn't do it. My days are too structured. I have phone calls, I have meetings, I have the softball league on Tuesdays and Thursdays. I can't be running to the restroom every five minutes. Plus, I feel like... I don't know, I feel like I'm already punishing my body enough with the starving and the intense hiking and running. Adding chemicals or pills on top of that just seems like it would be crossing a line that I really don't want to cross. So, no, I just stick to skipping meals and working out until I can barely stand. That's my way of dealing with it. No pills, no laxatives, nothing like that.
Have you ever engaged in any behaviors to try to compensate for the calories you consumed during these episodes, other than restricting your food intake and exercising?

No, I haven't. I mean, I really think I've covered everything I do. It's just the starving the next day and the exercise. I know I just talked about the hiking and the softball, but really, that's it. I don't use anything else, no other tricks or anything. 

Like I said, I'm pretty structured. I wake up, I go to work, I deal with the insurance policies, and if it's the day after one of those nights, I just drink my ice water and I push myself on the trail or the field later. I guess some people might have other things they do, maybe weird diets or teas or something? I don't know, you see all those detox teas on Facebook, the ones the celebrities push, but I don't mess with any of that. I don't even like tea, honestly. I'm a coffee person, usually, though on those days I just stick to water because even coffee feels like... I don't know, like I don't deserve it? 

But yeah, no other behaviors. I don't use anything else to try and make up for it. Just the fasting and the running myself into the ground. It takes up so much of my energy and time just doing those two things, I can't imagine trying to fit anything else in. It's already like a full-time job on top of my actual full-time job, trying to manage the guilt and the calories and everything. So, no, nothing else. Just what we've already talked about.
Have you ever felt like you were trying to get rid of the calories from one of these eating episodes in any way other than through exercise or restricting your food intake?

No, honestly, I think we just went over this, didn't we? I mean, I really don't do anything else. It's just the not eating and the exercise. I know I've probably repeated myself a few times now, but that's really the long and short of it. I don't have any secret methods or hidden tricks up my sleeve. 

I guess when you ask it like that, it makes me stop and think if maybe I do something subconsciously? Like, maybe pacing around the house while I'm on the phone with a client, trying to burn an extra fifty calories? But no, I don't think that counts as trying to get rid of the calories from the night before, does it? That's just nervous energy, or maybe just wanting to stretch my legs because sitting in that ergonomic chair—which they swore would fix my lower back pain, but really hasn't done a thing, honestly—just gets so tedious. 

But as far as actually trying to undo the damage of eating all that food? No. Like I said before, I don't throw up, I don't take pills, I don't drink those weird detox teas. I just wake up the next morning feeling this heavy, awful pit in my stomach, and I tell myself, "Well, you really did it this time, so now you have to pay for it." And paying for it means not eating a single thing, just drinking my ice water, and then pushing myself on the trail or at softball practice until I feel like I'm going to collapse. That's the only way I know how to handle it. So, no, nothing else. Just the starving and the sweating.
Do you think your behaviors of restricting food intake and exercising excessively are intended to prevent weight gain?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, what other reason would there be, right? It's all about the math, really. It's like... well, it's like a bank account. Being in insurance, I look at everything as a matter of premiums and payouts, deficits and surpluses. When I have one of those nights where I just eat and eat, I'm basically overdrawing my account. So, yes, the entire point of what I do the next day is to prevent that from showing up on the scale. 

The next day after one of those nights, I wake up and I just feel this immense pressure to fix it. I'll tell myself I'm making up for it by skipping breakfast and lunch entirely. Which, honestly, skipping lunch at the office isn't the hardest thing in the world because half the time someone is microwaving leftover fish in the breakroom—Brenda does this at least twice a week, and I've told her it makes the whole sales floor smell, but she doesn't listen. Anyway, I just sit at my desk with my ice water, looking at policies, and I tell myself that the hunger is just me paying off the debt from the night before. 

But the food restriction isn't enough on its own to stop the weight gain, or at least I don't trust that it is. So I have to do the physical part, too. I'll make sure I take an extra-long hike, usually on the Pine Ridge trail because it has this brutal incline for the last mile and a half that just makes your lungs burn. Or, if it's a league night, I'll go to softball and I will just run myself into the dirt. I end up pushing harder at softball conditioning than anyone else out there, even when I'm completely exhausted. And at fifty, let me tell you, your knees really feel it when you're doing wind sprints or running bases like you're trying out for the Olympics. 

But I do it, even when I'm so tired I could just cry, because in my head, every drop of sweat is an ounce of weight I'm keeping off. If I didn't do all of that—if I just ate all that food and then went about a normal day—I'd blow up like a balloon. So, yes, the fasting, the extra-long hikes, pushing myself to the absolute limit at conditioning... it's 100% just to make sure I don't gain weight from what I did the night before.
Do you ever feel like your excessive exercise or restrictive eating is a direct response to the feelings of fullness or guilt after one of these eating episodes?

Oh, completely. The guilt is... I mean, it's really the whole driving force behind all of it, isn't it? Because you wake up—well, honestly, half the time it's hard to even get a good night's sleep when you're that full. You just lie there in the dark, feeling so heavy and bloated and just... disgusting, really. You just replay every single thing you put in your mouth, calculating it all over again. And then the alarm goes off, and I have to get ready to go into the office and deal with clients, and that's when the guilt really just hits me like a ton of bricks. It's like this dark cloud right over my head the minute I open my eyes. 

So, yes, it's absolutely a direct response to those feelings. The next day after one of those nights, I'll tell myself I'm making up for it by skipping breakfast and lunch. I just sit at my desk, drinking my water, and I let myself feel empty because the guilt tells me I have to. I have to fix that awful, full feeling from the night before. And then with the exercise, it's the exact same thing. I'll end up taking an extra-long hike, or I'll be out there pushing harder at softball conditioning, even when I'm just so incredibly tired. 

I mean, working a full day on absolutely zero food and then running bases at fifty years old? It's completely exhausting. My muscles ache, my knees are screaming at me, and I'm practically dead on my feet by the time I get home. But that guilt is just so loud. I can't just sit on the couch and rest, because all I'd be able to think about is how full I was the night before. So I just keep pushing and pushing, trying to sweat out the guilt, basically.
Do you think that if you didn't restrict your food intake and exercise excessively after these episodes, you would gain weight?

Oh, without a doubt. I mean, my metabolism just isn't what it used to be. When you hit fifty, it’s like your body just decides to hold onto every single calorie, especially when you spend eight hours a day sitting at a desk writing insurance policies. If I just ate all that food and then woke up the next morning, had a normal breakfast, and went about my day without doing anything to counteract it? I'd probably put on five pounds in a week. It terrifies me, honestly. 

That fear is exactly why I do all of this. Like I was saying earlier—and I know I keep coming back to this, but it really is just how my life works right now—the next day after one of those nights, I'll tell myself I'm making up for it by skipping breakfast and lunch entirely. I just have to. And then I have to do the physical part to make absolutely sure the scale doesn't move. I'll go take an extra-long hike up the trail, or I'll be out there pushing harder at softball conditioning than anyone else on the team, even when I'm just bone-tired. 

And I mean, I really am exhausted. I'm running on empty because I haven't eaten all day, but I force myself to do it anyway. If I didn't push through that exhaustion and do the fasting and the extra exercise, all that food from the night before would just stick right to me. I'd have to buy a whole new work wardrobe, and I just bought these really nice tailored slacks from Macy's for a big client meeting next month, and they fit perfectly right now. I can't afford to let myself go and ruin that. So, yes, if I didn't restrict my food and work out like crazy the next day, I know for an absolute fact that I would gain weight, and I just can't let that happen.
Do you ever have episodes where you eat a large amount of food in a short time without trying to make up for it afterwards?

Oh, no. No, never. I couldn't just... let it go. I mean, just the thought of doing that gives me anxiety. If I eat like that, I absolutely have to fix it. And honestly, for the past few months, this has been happening most weeks. It’s usually one or two nights a week where I just completely lose track and eat far, far more than I ever planned to. 

Like, I’ll sit down after a long day of dealing with policy renewals and angry clients—just last Tuesday I had this guy yelling at me on the phone for twenty minutes because his auto claim got denied over an excluded driver, which I explicitly warned him about when I wrote the policy, but they never listen, they just want someone to blame—and I’ll get home, and I’ll just eat. But there is absolutely no scenario where I just wake up the next morning and act like nothing happened. I always try to make up for it the next day. I’ll skip meals entirely, like I said, just sitting at my desk drinking my ice water while everyone else in the office is having their lunch, or I’ll make sure I’m exercising longer and harder than usual that evening. 

It’s a package deal, really. It's been like this pretty much every week for months now—one or two nights of overeating, and then the immediate response of skipping food and pushing myself to the limit on the trail or the softball field. I can't have one without the other, because like I said before, it’s a ledger. If there’s a massive debit, I have to balance it. I can't just leave the account in the red, I just can't. So, no, if it happens, the fasting and the extra exercise are absolutely guaranteed to follow.
How often do these episodes of eating in the evenings happen in a typical month?

Well, honestly, it's pretty much a regular thing now. For the past few months, it's been happening most weeks. I'd say it's usually one or two nights a week where things just completely get away from me and I eat far, far more than I ever intended to. 

And, you know, I know I've brought this up a few times already, but it really is just this cycle I'm stuck in. It's those one or two nights a week of just losing control, usually when I'm just so wound up from work. Like, if I've had to spend the whole afternoon explaining rate increases to people who just want to shoot the messenger, I get home and I'm just... done. So it happens those one or two nights, and then, without fail, the very next day is all about making up for it. I'll skip breakfast, skip lunch, just sit there with my water, and then I'll push myself out on the hiking trail or at softball practice until I can barely stand. So, yeah, in a typical month, you're looking at maybe four to eight of these episodes, and every single one of them is followed by the fasting and the extra exercise. It's just... it's most weeks. It's just how my weeks go now.
Do these episodes of eating in the evenings, followed by restricting food intake and excessive exercise, happen at least once a week for at least three months?

Yes, absolutely. Like I was just saying, it really has been going on for the past few months now, and it's definitely at least once a week. Usually one or two nights a week, honestly. I'll have that night where I just completely lose track of everything and eat way, way more than I ever meant to—like I said, usually after a really stressful day of dealing with angry clients and policy renewals—and then the very next day, without fail, I'm doing everything I can to fix it. 

I'll skip breakfast, I'll skip lunch, I'll just sit at my desk with my ice water while everyone else is eating, and then I'll go out and push myself to the absolute limit on the hiking trail or at softball conditioning. And it's been this exact same routine, week in and week out, for months. I can't even remember the last time I went a full week without this happening. It's just become this exhausting cycle that I'm completely stuck in, and it's been exactly like this for at least three months, probably more. It's just... it's every week. It really is.

doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Eating_Large_Amount
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is that some evenings after work, especially when I've been strict all day, I end up eating way more than I meant to, like dinner, then cereal, crackers, leftovers, and sweets all within a couple hours.

patient.answer:
Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Well, it's... it's a bit hard to talk about, but I guess I'm here because of what's been happening in the evenings. You see, I sell insurance, which is a lot of sitting at a desk and talking on the phone, and I really, really try to be so good during the day. I'm very strict with myself from the moment I wake up—I'll just have something small, keep it very disciplined. But then... then I get home after work, and it's like a switch just flips in my brain. 

I'll walk in the door, put my purse down, and I just start eating, and I end up eating way, way more than I ever intended to. It usually starts out okay, just making a normal dinner, but then... then I'll have a bowl of cereal. And then I'll open a box of crackers. And then I'm digging into whatever leftovers are sitting in the fridge, and then I absolutely have to have something sweet, so I'm finding cookies or whatever sweets I have around the kitchen... and this all happens so fast, just all within a couple of hours. Oh, gosh, yes. Absolutely. The guilt is just... it's immense. It's like this heavy, wet blanket just drops right over me the very second that spell breaks and I realize what I've just done. I'll be standing there in the kitchen, or maybe I've finally made it to the couch, and I just look at the empty boxes or the wrappers, and I just think, "Why? Why did you do this again?" It's this awful, sinking feeling of failure, really, because I know better. I'm a fifty-year-old woman, I manage complex insurance policies all day, I should be able to manage my own dinner, right? So, yes, I feel like I've done something terribly wrong. 

And because I feel so guilty, so ashamed of it, I always... well, I have this whole routine the next day to try and fix it. I'll tell myself I'm making up for it. So the next morning, I'll wake up and I'll just completely skip breakfast. Won't even look at the toaster. If I didn't push through that exhaustion and do the fasting and the extra exercise, all that food from the night before would just stick right to me. I'd have to buy a whole new work wardrobe, and I just bought these really nice tailored slacks from Macy's for a big client meeting next month, and they fit perfectly right now. I can't afford to let myself go and ruin that. So, yes, if I didn't restrict my food and work out like crazy the next day, I know for an absolute fact that I would gain weight, and I just can't let that happen.

Oh, no. No, never. I couldn't just... let it go. I mean, just the thought of doing that gives me anxiety. If I eat like that, I absolutely have to fix it. Like, I’ll sit down after a long day of dealing with policy renewals and angry clients—just last Tuesday I had this guy yelling at me on the phone for twenty minutes because his auto claim got denied over an excluded driver, which I explicitly warned him about when I wrote the policy, but they never listen, they just want someone to blame—and I’ll get home, and I’ll just eat. But there is absolutely no scenario where I just wake up the next morning and act like nothing happened. I always try to make up for it the next day. I’ll skip meals entirely, like I said, just sitting at my desk drinking my ice water while everyone else in the office is having their lunch, or I’ll make sure I’m exercising longer and harder than usual that evening. 

It’s a package deal, really. It's been like this pretty much every week for months now—one or two nights of overeating, and then the immediate response of skipping food and pushing myself to the limit on the trail or the softball field. I can't have one without the other, because like I said before, it’s a ledger. If there’s a massive debit, I have to balance it. I can't just leave the account in the red, I just can't. So, no, if it happens, the fasting and the extra exercise are absolutely guaranteed to follow.
